slides.title: Learning Outcomes
slides.text:
Learning Outcome

•  Explain the structure and operating principles of a SCARA manipulator.
•  Select appropriate link dimensions, actuators, and transmission systems for a
  SCARA robot.
•  Develop forward and inverse kinematic models using the DH convention.
•  Analyze workspace, Jacobian, velocity relationships, and manipulator dynamics.
•  Design trajectory planning and closed-loop sensor feedback systems.
•  Evaluate industrial SCARA robot architectures and controller configurations.

•  Perform complete manipulator design calculations
   including sizing, component selection, and cost estimation.

slides.title: SCARA: Structure and Applications
slides.text:
What is a SCARA Robot?
•  SCARA - Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm.
•   It is selectively compliant — rigid in Z (vertical) yet
    flexible in the X-Y plane for insertion tasks.
•  4-DOF Structure: 2 revolute joints in horizontal plane
   + 1 prismatic (Z) + 1 rotary at wrist.
•  High-Speed Motion: Cycle times under 0.4 s. Ideal for
   high-throughput pick-and-place on conveyors.
•  Repeatability:±0.01mm repeatability is achievable.
    Critical for semiconductor and micro-assembly tasks.
•  AI Readiness: Embedded vision, force-torque sensing,
   and neural IK make SCARA a prime AI platform.
•  Industry Use: PCB assembly, drug dispensing, solar cell
   handling, bottle capping, screw driving.

                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: SCARA expands Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm; relatively rigid Z and compliant XY for insertion. Four DOF: two vertical-axis planar revolutes, vertical prismatic joint, wrist revolute. Slide claims cycles below 0.4 s and repeatability ±0.01 mm as examples, not universal specifications. Lists vision, force-torque sensing and neural IK as AI-readiness features, not mandatory components. Applications PCB assembly, drug dispensing, solar-cell handling, bottle capping, screwdriving. Diagram shows base/frame0, d1 upward height, links l1/l2, vertical z0/z1/z2/z3 arrows up, d3 dimension arrow down from arm to wrist, coincident O3/O4 wrist frames, θ1/θ2/θ4. Potential d3-axis convention must be reconciled with later DH table rather than silently changed.

slides.title: Actuation Systems & Power Transmission
slides.text:
Actuation Systems & Power Transmission

•  Each SCARA joint requires a specific actuator–
   transmission combination optimised for speed,
   precision, and backlash.
  Joint 1 (Shoulder)
  •  Actuator: AC Servo Motor
  •  Drive: Harmonic Drive (strain-wave gear); Zero backlash; 100:1 reduction; High torque
     density; Essential for smooth, accurate shoulder rotation.
  •  Torque: 20–80 Nm, Resolution: <1 arcsec
  Joint 2 (Elbow)
  •  Actuator: AC Servo Motor
  •  Drive: Harmonic Drive or Spur Gear; Harmonic preferred; spur
    gear used for lower-cost designs. Elbow must be lighter than
     shoulder.
  •  Torque: 10–40 Nm; Inertia match: 1:4

                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: J1 AC servo plus harmonic strain-wave100:1 drive; source says zero backlash, essential smooth accurate shoulder,20–80 N m, resolution<1 arcsec. J2 AC servo plus harmonic or lower-cost spur, elbow should be lighter than shoulder,10–40 N m and inertia match1:4 without specifying numerator/reference shaft. Same schematic. Absolute zero-backlash/essential claims need qualified interpretation; inertia ratio cannot support a numerical derivation until definitions are supplied.

slides.title: Actuation Systems & Power Transmission (Continued)
slides.text:
Actuation Systems & Power Transmission (Continued) :

Joint 3 (Z-axis)
•  Actuator: AC Servo or Stepper
•  Drive: Ball Screw + Linear Guide; ball screw converts
   rotary to linear with 95% efficiency; preloaded nut
   eliminates axial backlash.
•   Pitch: 5–20 mm; Stiffness: >200 N/μm

Joint 4 (Wrist)
•  Actuator: Servo Motor
•  Drive: Direct Drive or Belt Pulley; Direct drive for highest
   accuracy. Belt drive reduces wrist inertia — critical for
   high-speed operation.
•  Torque: 1–5 Nm; Speed: up to 2000 rpm


                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: J3 AC servo or stepper, ball screw+linear guide, rotary-linear conversion95% efficiency, preloaded nut source says eliminates axial backlash, pitch5–20 mm, stiffness>200 N/μm. J4 servo direct drive or belt pulley, direct drive highest accuracy claim, remote belt drive lowers wrist inertia, torque1–5 N m and speed up to2000 rpm. Same labeled schematic. Treat efficiency and limits as supplied design values; lead equals pitch only for single-start screw. Preload does not guarantee zero compliance.

slides.title: Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) Parameters for SCARA
slides.text:
Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) Parameters for SCARA

  •  The DH convention assigns coordinate frames to each
     joint using 4 parameters.
          𝒊         𝜶𝒊−𝟏       𝒂𝒊−𝟏         𝒅𝒊          𝜽𝒊
       1         0         0          𝑑1         𝜃1
       2         0             𝑙1         0          𝜃2
       3         0             𝑙2       𝑑3(variable)     0
       4         0         0         0          𝜃4
•     𝑙1​,​ 𝑙2 : horizontal arm lengths of link 1 and link 2.
•  𝑑1 : fixed vertical offset from the base to the first arm plane.
•  𝑑3 : prismatic joint variable (vertical motion of the SCARA).
•  𝜃1, 𝜃2, 𝜃4 : revolute joint angles about the vertical 𝑧-axes.



                                                                                                             9

slides.title: Forward Kinematics: Numerical Example
slides.text:
FORWARD KINEMATICS :
•  End-effector position equations:
• 𝑥= 𝑙1 cos 𝜃1 + 𝑙2 cos 𝜃1 + 𝜃2  ;
• 𝑦= 𝑙1 sin 𝜃1 + 𝑙2sin 𝜃1 + 𝜃2  ;
• 𝑧= 𝑑1 −𝑑3; 𝜙= 𝜃1 + 𝜃2 + 𝜃4
•  Manipulator dimensions: 𝑙1= 250mm; 𝑙2 = 200mm
•  Assume: 𝜃1 = 45∘; 𝜃2 = 30∘; 𝑑1 = 400mm; 𝑑3 = 80mm; 𝜃4 = 15∘
•   Substituting,
• 𝑥= 228.6mm; 𝑦= 369.7mm; 𝑧= 320mm; 𝜙= 90∘
•  Thus the desired pick-and-place position is achieved
   within the required workspace.

visualInspection.notes: Equations x=l1cosθ1+l2cos(θ1+θ2), y=l1sinθ1+l2sin(θ1+θ2), z=d1−d3,φ=θ1+θ2+θ4. Givenl1=250 mm,l2=200 mm,θ1=45°,θ2=30°,d1=400 mm,d3=80 mm,θ4=15°. Printedresultx228.6 mm,y369.7 mm,z320 mm,φ90°. Needexactcheck: likelyroundingofx/y, preserveprintedversuscomputed.

• 𝑉Θ ሶΘ represents Coriolis and centrifugal effects

slides.title: Vision Integration and Condition Monitoring
slides.text:
•  Vision Integration
   – The robot supports integrated two-dimensional and three-dimensional
      machine vision systems.
   – Capabilities include: Part localization, Barcode identification, Defect
       inspection
   – Coordinate transformation Flexible feeder guidance
   – Vision information is transformed into robot coordinates and supplied to
      the inverse kinematic solver for motion generation.
•  Condition Monitoring
   – The controller continuously monitors: Motor current,
        Joint position, Joint velocity, Temperature, Vibration
   – collected data is used for fault diagnosis &
      maintenance scheduling.
   – Monitoring of gearbox and bearing health improves
      system availability and reduces unexpected downtime.

slides.text:

   applications.
•  Discussed mechanical design, link geometry, actuator selection, and power

•  Analyzed industrial case studies of Epson T6 and FANUC SR-6iA SCARA robots.
•  Completed the design and component selection of a 4-DOF
  SCARA manipulator for high-speed assembly applications.

•  Evaluated cost distribution, controller architecture, and
   system integration considerations.
